- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.18) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >+5% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope afterward.
- If sentiment is positive (≥0.36) and price is trending upward, model frequently overestimates near-term gains; cap forecast growth at 3–5% above recent high.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.18–0.53), model exhibits mean-reversion bias — forecast often lags true price by 1–3 days; shift forecast 1–2 days ahead with slight upward bias.
- In low-sentiment environments (sentiment <0.10), model underestimates volatility and fails to capture downward spikes; add 2–3% buffer below recent low to account for sudden drops.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early period (first 7–10 days) and underestimates late period (last 7–10 days); apply asymmetric smoothing: reduce early forecast by 2–5% and increase late forecast by 2–5% to align with true volatility decay.
